Eggs of the Coconut crab Birgus latro, incubated at a water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], complete embryonic development and hatch after approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days]. This incubation period is relatively short for a decapod of its eventual size, and the resulting larvae are released into the ocean where they enter a planktonic phase. The newly hatched zoea, emerging from an egg with a dry weight of just 0.00041 grams [Wwb = 0.00041 grams], begin a protracted developmental journey through five zoeal instars followed by a single, amphibious glaucothoe stage. The entire duration from hatching to the completion of metamorphosis into a benthic juvenile is 49 days  when the water is maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This surprisingly long larval period, totaling 28 days for the planktonic zoeal stages and an additional 21 days for the glaucothoe, exposes the tiny post-larvae to substantial risks of offshore advection and predation before they can successfully recruit to coastal habitat.

Field surveys on Christmas Island have provided detailed morphometric data for wild Coconut crabs, revealing substantial sexual dimorphism in adult body size. Mature females attain a maximum thoracic length of 5 centimeters [Li = 5 centimeters], whereas mature males can reach a significantly larger ultimate thoracic length of 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters]. This pronounced difference in maximum adult dimensions likely reflects sexual selection for larger male body size, which confers an advantage in contests over access to reproductive females. In contrast, the thoracic length at which the first signs of sexual maturation are evident in both sexes is 2.45 centimeters [Lp = 2.45 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from this thoracic length relative to adult dimensions, is 118 grams [Wwp = 118 grams], marking the threshold at which individuals begin to allocate resources toward gonad development rather than exclusively toward somatic growth.

In a comprehensive mark-recapture study on the Ryukyu Islands, researchers tracked the growth of juvenile Coconut crabs over several years. Under the warm thermal conditions typical of these subtropical environments, which generally average 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the crustaceans exhibited a steady and predictable growth trajectory. At approximately 2.5 years of age, individuals were recorded as having a mean thoracic length of 0.75 centimeters , a size that reflects the relatively slow, energy-conserving growth strategy characteristic of terrestrial hermit crabs at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This measured length provides a crucial benchmark for calibrating growth curves for the species, as the early juvenile phase is a critical period of high mortality. The long developmental period before reaching the size necessary to avoid most predators is a key feature of the life history of Birgus latro, which is known for its exceptional longevity and delayed reproduction compared to most marine decapods.

Reproductive output in the Coconut crab has been quantified from captive breeding colonies, where berried females were maintained under controlled conditions. At a stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum reproductive rate was assessed by counting the average number of eggs extruded per clutch and the frequency of spawning events. Ovigerous females were observed to produce approximately 378 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 378 eggs per day] over the course of the breeding season, a remarkably high fecundity that compensates for the extensive larval mortality incurred during the prolonged planktonic phase. This impressive daily fecundity, sustained by stored lipid reserves and efficient foraging, enables a single female to release hundreds of thousands of viable larvae into the surrounding waters over the span of a single reproductive cycle. The high output is critical for maintaining population stability on islands where terrestrial predation pressure on juveniles is intense.

The exceptionally slow life history of Birgus latro culminates in an extraordinarily long lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching a maximum longevity of approximately 100 years [am = approximately 100 years] when reared under the warm ambient conditions of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] in their native habitat. This extreme lifespan, exceeding that of many large vertebrates, is accompanied by a similarly protracted period of development. The time since birth at which the first signs of gonadal activity and functional sexual maturity appear is 5 years [tp = 5 years], meaning that individuals do not begin contributing to the next generation until they have spent half a decade growing and accumulating reserves at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This delayed maturation, combined with the enormous adult size of the species, anchors a life-history strategy built on high survival at the cost of very slow growth. The ultimate wet weight for the largest adult females is 1000 grams [Wwi = 1000 grams], while the most massive adult males documented reached a staggering 4100 grams [Wwi = 4100 grams], a weight that highlights the profound sexual dimorphism underlying their reproductive ecology.
